description: Test your knowledge of PA G5 | Immunopathology & Amyloidosis.

cards.text: What is the 'missing-self' hypothesis and which cells use this mechanism?
cards.answer: NK cells kill target cells that lack MHC class I expression. Virus-infected and tumour cells often downregulate MHC I to escape CTL, but this makes them vulnerable to NK cell recognition. This is the absence of 'self' signal that triggers killing.

tip.tip: MHC I present = safe. No MHC I = missing self = NK kill

cards.text: Compare the four Th helper cell subsets: which subset produces IFN-γ, which produces IL-17, and what are their main targets?
cards.answer: Th1: IFN-γ (activates macrophages vs intracellular pathogens). Th2: IL-4, IL-5 (B-cell help, IgE, allergy). Th17: IL-17 (neutrophil recruitment vs fungi/bacteria). Treg: IL-10, TGF-β (suppress excess responses).

cards.text: What are the key differences between MHC class I and MHC class II in terms of expression, peptide source, and T-cell recognition?
cards.answer: MHC I: all nucleated cells; endogenous peptides (viral, tumour); CD8+ CTL. MHC II: professional APCs only; exogenous peptides (bacterial, ingested); CD4+ helper T cells.

tip.tip: Class I = all cells, endogenous (CTL patrol). Class II = APCs only, exogenous (T help others)

cards.text: Describe the primary vs secondary immune response in terms of onset, antibody type, titre, and affinity maturation.
cards.answer: Primary: 7–14 day lag, IgM dominates, low titre, low affinity (no maturation yet). Secondary: 1–3 day lag, IgG dominates, high titre, high affinity. Memory B and T cells account for speed and quality.

tip.tip: 1st time = slow IgM. 2nd time = fast IgG (remember = secondary)

cards.text: Which innate immunity components are activated immediately (within hours) at an injury site?
cards.answer: Physical barriers (skin, mucosae), neutrophils (6–8 h), macrophages (24–48 h), complement system (C3b opsonin, MAC), and the inflammatory cascade (vasodilation, cytokines).

tip.tip: Barriers first, then PMN rush in, macro clean up later. Complement & inflammation glue it together.

cards.text: What mediates Type I (Immediate) hypersensitivity, what is the onset time, and give a clinical example.
cards.answer: IgE + mast cells (and basophils). Onset: minutes. Examples: anaphylaxis, acute allergic reactions, atopy, food allergy. Mast cells release histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins upon cross-linking of IgE-Fc receptors by antigen.

tip.tip: Type I = IgE-mast = Minutes = Anaphylaxis. Remember: 'I for Immediate and IgE'

cards.text: What is Type II (Antibody-mediated) hypersensitivity, what antibodies are involved, and what is a clinical example?
cards.answer: Antibody (IgG or IgM) binds cell-surface antigens → complement activation, ADCC, or opsonisation. Onset: hours. Examples: autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, Graves' disease, pemphigus vulgaris.

tip.tip: Type II = antibody vs cell = destruction (haemolysis, cell lysis). Think cytotoxic.

cards.text: What three main products does the complement system generate, and what is their primary function?
cards.answer: C3b (opsonin — tags pathogens for phagocytosis), C3a and C5a (anaphylatoxins — recruit and activate phagocytes and mast cells), C5b-9 (membrane attack complex — lysing pathogens). The cascade amplifies innate response and bridges to adaptive immunity.

tip.tip: Complement = C3b opsonise + C3a/C5a chemotaxis + C5b-9 lysis. The 'three Cs'
